Readings / The gender gap is measured. Its explanation is still open.
Reading

What do we know about the gender gap in account ownership, and what would it take to explain it?

The gender gap is measured. Its explanation is still open.

Report an error

The latest Findex observation shows a large gap between women’s and men’s account ownership inside a system where few adults of either sex have an account. The evidence tells us where the disparity is. It does not yet tell us which barriers produce it.

Evidence periodGlobal Findex, Yemen fieldwork 7 November 2022 – 9 January 2023
Last reviewed26 September 2026

What not to conclude

The measured gap does not establish its causes, the causal contribution of any proposed mechanism, or the size of the gap in 2026; a plausible mechanism is not an established causal explanation.

01The mechanism is still open02Measure the journey, not only the endpoint03What would change this reading?04Trace the evidence05Sources06Related measurement priorities07Related readings

In the latest Global Findex wave for Yemen, 18.3% of men and 5.4% of women aged 15 and over in the areas surveyed had an account, a gap of 12.9 percentage points. This is a valid comparison within one survey wave. It is a measured disparity, and it is not, by itself, an explanation.

The gap also sits inside a low-access system. Overall account ownership in the same wave is 11.9%, and men’s measured level is low too. The sharper question is therefore:

Why does an already low-access financial system reach women so much less than men?

That moves attention away from “fixing women” and towards the conditions under which access is produced.

The mechanism is still open

Plausible mechanisms include income, employment, identity documents, phone ownership and control, distance, mobility, trust, household decision-making, provider practice and product design. For Yemen these are hypotheses to test, not findings; the current evidence does not divide the 12.9-point gap among them.

The same survey records a gap of 9.0 percentage points between adults in the poorest 40% of households by income (6.5%) and those in the richest 60% (15.5%). That does not explain the gender gap. It shows why one-dimensional explanations are risky.

Measure the journey, not only the endpoint

Account ownership is one point on a longer path. Better measurement would ask whether a woman can open an account, whether she controls the device and the account, whether she uses it and returns to it, what it costs her, whether it works, whether she can obtain redress, whether she decides how it is used, and whether it improves something she values.

Provider data can follow the same path from the other side: applications, approvals, rejections, active use, dormancy, balances, credit, complaints, fraud, resolution and exit, each with a visible denominator.

What would change this reading?

A current representative survey design for Yemen that combines up-to-date sex-disaggregated measures of access, use, quality and protection; the variables that could explain the gap, collected in the same survey; comparisons among different groups of women; and provider-side customer funnels.

The gap tells us where to investigate. It does not tell us which intervention to choose.

If we can measure the gap but cannot yet locate where women are being lost — at access, activation, use, persistence or quality — how can we know that an intervention is aimed at the right problem?

Related measurement priorities

Each priority below would supply evidence that this Reading says is missing; the link does not mean the priority would settle the Reading.

Measurement priorityP0 · People / Equity
Financial inclusion across population groups: measure disparities before explaining them
Within the same survey wave, account ownership differs by 12.9 percentage points between women (5.4%) and men (18.3%), and by 9.0 percentage points between adults in the poorest 40% (6.5%) and the richest 60% (15.5%) by household income. Comparable current differences by age group and displacement status are not established in the evidence base, and the contribution of identity, device, income, geography, trust and household constraints to any measured disparity is not established.
Evidence needed: Representative or clearly bounded disaggregated quantitative evidence to measure subgroup outcomes, with linked mechanism variables and qualitative or stronger causal designs where explanation is required.
Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would show which subgroup differences are actually measured and would allow plausible mechanisms to be tested without treating untested explanations as causes.
Open this measurement priority
Measurement priorityP1 · Identity / Digital access
Digital onboarding and identity journeys
KYC and e-money rules are documented, but this resource lacks journey-level evidence on attempts, completion, rejection, abandonment, time and cost.
Evidence needed: Journey-level administrative or survey data across onboarding stages: identity and KYC verification, attempts, completion, rejection, abandonment, time and cost.
Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would identify where users leave or fail the onboarding journey and which frictions are associated with those points.
Open this measurement priority

Related readings

Evidence periodProvider data 2016–2019, from a 2020 study of five e-money providers
When does digital growth become durable use?
Historical evidence from Yemen records a large base of e-money accounts by 2019 alongside dormancy, one-off use and a transaction mix still closely tied to cash. The open question is whether people choose to return to digital finance and find enough value to keep using it.
Evidence periodGlobal Findex fieldwork November 2022 – January 2023 · point-of-sale (POS) counts March 2025 – June 2026 · institutional records June–August 2026
The system is changing. What has reached people?
Yemen’s rules, institutions and payment infrastructure have moved faster than its representative evidence about people. The gap between the two is not an answer to guess; it is the next thing to measure.
